Ethnicity
As previously noted, recent data suggest that Hispanics are at 
higher risk than non-Hispanic whites, whereas blacks are at 
lower risk for low bone density (Looker et al, 2012). However, 
non-Hispanic whites suffer more fractures than other racial or 
ethnic groups. Nevertheless, the incidence of fracture has de-
clined in all racial and ethnic groups except Hispanics (Wright 
et al, 2012).
Limited Weight-Bearing Exercise
Maintenance of healthy bone requires exposure to weight-
bearing pressures. A good diet plus exercise from roughly ages 
10 to 20 years is particularly important for skeletal growth, ac-
crual of bone mass, and increased femoral bone dimensions 
(Iuliano-Burns et al, 2005). Physical activity, especially upper 
body activities, is thought to contribute to an increase in bone 
mass or density (Chubak et al, 2006). Lack of exercise and a 
sedentary mode of living also may contribute to bone loss,
